episodes.183577: A deamplifying mid level shortwave with dewpoints in the 70s and decent instability brought scattered thunderstorms and widespread flash flooding to Massachusetts and Rhode Island. There were many streets closed, many cars stranded in flood waters, and several houses with flooded basements or first floors.
episodes.183578: A deamplifying mid level shortwave with dewpoints in the 70s and decent instability brought scattered thunderstorms and widespread flash flooding to Rhode Island and Massachusetts. There were many streets closed, many cars stranded in flood waters, and several houses with flooded basements or first floors.
episodes.183790: Broad troughing and mid-level dry air extended down from the Great Lakes, providing weak but favorable forcing across South Carolina for convection, allowing a sub-severe thunderstorm to produce gusty winds and some damage in Cayce.
episodes.183912: Prefrontal trough ahead of cold front sparks scattered thunderstorms, with one thunderstorm maintaining severe strength for a couple of hours. This thunderstorm produced damaging winds during that time.
episodes.184238: An active period of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms resulted in several reports of wind damage.  Most of the damage occurred on September 7th as a cluster of severe storms moved through Tallahassee.  In addition, a significant downburst with winds estimated around 85 mph occurred near Spring Creek in Wakulla county.
episodes.184447: Unsettled weather was on the docket each afternoon from September 9th through the 12th across West Virginia as a result of a stationary frontal boundary residing over the area. While severe parameters were not impressive during this time frame, afternoon thunderstorms had enough gumption to promote isolated tree and power line damage across parts of the state. High moisture levels festering over these several days also resulted in high water issues along local roads, especially in Raleigh County, where flood prone areas in the Beckley area took on a decent amount of street flooding on September 10th. Convection was primarily diurnally driven during this time, so the severe and flash flooding concerns quickly tapered down after sunset each day.
episodes.184612: A short-wave trough moved across the area during the evening which enhanced thunderstorm strength where the sea breezes converged over a moist and unstable airmass.
episodes.184744: Training showers and thunderstorms developed along a slow moving frontal boundary stretching from Connecticut to Southwest Maine on the evening of the 11th. The anomalously moist airmass caused moderate to heavy widespread rain of 1 to 3 inches. A localized axis of heavy rainfall between 4 to 6 inches extended from central Massachusetts across the Stateline and into Nashua, New Hampshire. Flash flooding developed over Nashua, Hollis, and Hudson with numerous water rescues and flooded basements.
episodes.184923: Many severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening across southeast New Mexico and the Permian Basin. These thunderstorms developed within strong mid-level flow aloft as a trough passed across the Midwest and a cold front sagged into the region. Damaging wind gusts and large hail were observed with thunderstorms across the region.
episodes.185072: Severe thunderstorms produced wind damage and quarter size hail around the Orlando metro area.
episodes.185163: Scattered thunderstorms developed across parts of Central Alabama during the afternoon and evening hours on September 12th, producing tree damage in parts of Jefferson, St. Clair, and Randolph counties.
episodes.185257: Heavy thunderstorms developed in an unstable and moist environment on September 11th, 2023 and produced flash flooding in Connecticut. Thunderstorms developed along a stationary front that was draped over the area in an environment with 2000-2500 J/kg of SBCAPE and 1.7-1.9 inches of PWAT. The thunderstorms produced rainfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour and a total of 1-3 inches of rainfall in a couple of hours.
episodes.185564: The combination of an upper level trough of low pressure moving across the area and some instability resulted in a few severe thunderstorms. The severe storms produced large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.185644: An approaching cold front from the Michigan and Mid-Mississippi Valley region led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms. These storms first developed across the western Piedmont and tracked east-northeast toward the Sandhills and Coastal Plain in the late-evening and overnight hours. Several reports of flash flooding and damaging winds were reported in Guilford and Forsyth Counties.
episodes.185664: Many severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening across southeast New Mexico and the Permian Basin. These thunderstorms developed within strong mid-level flow aloft as a trough passed across the Midwest and a cold front sagged into the region. Damaging wind gusts and large hail were observed with thunderstorms across the region.
episodes.185709: The synoptic pattern was characterized by strong westerly flow aloft situated across most of the Desert Southwest with embedded shortwave energy providing the main source for rising motion. Above normal moisture was present with PWATs in excess of 1.5 across most of central and southwestern AZ. The available moisture in combination with the daytime heating led to the development of moderate instability  with MLCAPE in excess of 1000 J/KG. The strong westerly flow aloft led to strong vertical shear with 0-6 KM shear values ranging between 30-40 knots. All of these factors led to a very favorable environment for the development of strong to severe thunderstorms across portions of south-central AZ. Scattered thunderstorms started to develop by the early afternoon hours of the 12th with multiple rounds continuing into the evening hours. One severe thunderstorm in particular developed near the Buckeye area, became supercellular, and tracked generally eastward affecting areas such as Goodyear, Glendale, Phoenix, Scottsdale, Mesa and Apache Junction, causing extensive straight-line wind damage along its path. Additional thunderstorms developed just east of the Phoenix metro area during the overnight and early morning hours of the 13th, with the main impact being isolated flash flooding.
episodes.185800: Isolated severe thunderstorm in advance of a cold front produced damaging winds across portions of south central Virginia.
episodes.185894: A flash flood event occurred in the Duluth area during the late evening of September 11th into the early morning hours of the 12th. An area of thunderstorms developed over Duluth during the evening hours and continued to backbuild over the hillside for a few hours before another area of rainfall pushed in from the west and helped push the backbuilding storms out over the lake. Rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches fell over a small area at the top of the Duluth hillside in the Chester Creek basin in the area around College of St. Scholastica. This sent a surge of water downstream on Chester Creek down the Duluth hillside just to the east of downtown. The creek is generally underground for most of its run down the hill to Lake Superior, but the volume of water overwhelmed the tunnels and led to fast-flowing water on the surface. This resulted in a a few rescues by the fire department as the water cut-off access to an apartment building. At the bottom of the hill, Interstate 35 runs through a series of tunnels and the runoff from Chester Creek collected in the tunnels leading to a closure of the highway for a few hours until the water subsided.
episodes.185897: A cold front associated with an upper level trough triggered the development of thunderstorms across Southside Virginia in the afternoon and evening. Warm air advection ahead of the front steadily increased through the day, and increased moisture over the area. This environment led to localized damaging winds gusts from storms.
episodes.185902: North and Central Texas were situated beneath the eastern flank of a mid and upper level high pressure ridge during the early to middle part of the month. Multiple disturbances within the flow aloft, along with a weak surface front, resulted in thunderstorm development each day during the weekend of Sept 8-11. A few of these storms became severe with mainly damaging downburst winds.
episodes.185990: Respectable instability and moderate lift from a digging upper-level trough initiated scattered thunderstorms across portions of North and Central GA. A couple of storms in the Northwest ATL Metro were able to become strong with damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.186243: Scattered thunderstorms along with a few storm clusters developed across upstate South Carolina throughout the afternoon. A few of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.186244: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across western North Carolina during the late afternoon. A couple of storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in the northern Piedmont.

Thunderstorms over parts of Duluth dropped upwards of 3 to 6 inches of rain over a localized area focused on the Chester Creek basin over a period of 2 to 3 hours. The highest rainfall totals were located at the top of the hill in the College of St. Scholastica area. Flash flooding was reported upstream from this location along Arrowhead Road where 3 to 6 inches of water was flowing over the road where Chester Creek passed under the road. As the surge of water flowed downstream, it damaged walkways along the creek and sent 2 to 5 inches of water onto side streets and Kenwood Avenue. Chester Creek runs through tunnels for much of its trip down the Duluth hillside and this volume of water overwhelmed the tunnels sending a large stream of rapidly flowing water 3 to 10 inches deep down the hill. This affected a few apartment buildings in the vicinity of 7th Avenue and 3rd Street which required a few rescues/evacuations of lower level residents and pets in the buildings by the fire department. Interstate 35 runs through tunnels underground at the base of the hill and the water surging down the hillside began to collect in the tunnels. Standing and flowing water in the tunnels resulted in the closure of the tunnels for a period. Water of at least 4 to 6 inches in depth was covering the southbound lanes in spots. The water receded during the early morning hours of the 12th with cleanup occurring over the remainder of the week.

Heavy rainfall from backbuilding thunderstorms over Duluth led to 2 to 5 inches of rainfall in 2-3 hours. As the water rushed down the hillside to Lake Superior, it scoured out gravel alleys and sent around 1,000 cubic yards of construction debris, including sand, dirt, rock and other materials, onto Superior Street at the base of the hill. Superior Street at First Avenue East was closed for much of the 12th as crews worked to remove the piles of debris using heavy machinery.
